lessons.title: Introduction to Data Interpretation
lessons.description: Understand how to read, analyze and compare numerical data in placement aptitude questions.
lessons.content:
Data Interpretation (DI) is the process of understanding numerical information presented through tables, charts, graphs and written datasets.

DI questions commonly test percentages, ratios, averages, differences, trends and logical comparisons.

Important formulas:
Percentage = (Part / Total) × 100
Average = Sum of Values / Number of Values
Percentage Change = ((New Value - Old Value) / Old Value) × 100
Ratio = Quantity A / Quantity B

Example dataset: Students placed in three departments.
Computer Science = 80
Electronics = 60
Mechanical = 40

Total placements = 80 + 60 + 40 = 180.

Computer Science placement share = (80/180) × 100 = 44.44% approximately.

Ratio of Computer Science to Mechanical placements = 80:40 = 2:1.

Difference between Computer Science and Electronics placements = 20.

Important steps:
1. Read the title and units.
2. Identify the relevant rows or categories.
3. Determine what the question asks.
4. Select the appropriate formula.
5. Calculate and verify the result.

Placement tip: Avoid performing calculations before identifying exactly which values are required.

lessons.title: Tabular Data Interpretation
lessons.description: Solve aptitude questions using rows, columns, totals and comparisons in tables.
lessons.content:
Tabular Data Interpretation presents numerical information in rows and columns.

Example: Quarterly sales in ₹ thousands.

Quarter | Product A | Product B
Q1 | 40 | 30
Q2 | 50 | 45
Q3 | 60 | 50
Q4 | 70 | 55

Total Product A sales = 40 + 50 + 60 + 70 = 220 thousand.
Total Product B sales = 30 + 45 + 50 + 55 = 180 thousand.

Combined annual sales = 400 thousand.

Average quarterly sales of Product A = 220/4 = 55 thousand.

Product A sales increased from 40 thousand in Q1 to 70 thousand in Q4.
Percentage increase = ((70 - 40)/40) × 100 = 75%.

Difference between total Product A and Product B sales = 40 thousand.

Ratio of total sales A:B = 220:180 = 11:9.

Common question patterns:
1. Find row or column totals.
2. Compare categories.
3. Calculate percentage contributions.
4. Find maximum and minimum values.
5. Calculate averages and growth rates.

Placement tip: Pay attention to units such as thousands, lakhs, crores and percentages.

lessons.title: Bar Graph and Line Graph Interpretation
lessons.description: Analyze comparisons, trends and percentage changes from bar charts and line graphs.
lessons.content:
Bar graphs use rectangular bars to compare quantities across categories. Line graphs connect data points to show changes across an ordered sequence, often time.

Example: Company revenue in ₹ lakhs.
2021 = 20
2022 = 25
2023 = 30
2024 = 45
2025 = 60

Total revenue across five years = 180 lakhs.

Average annual revenue = 180/5 = 36 lakhs.

Revenue growth from 2021 to 2022 = ((25 - 20)/20) × 100 = 25%.

Revenue growth from 2023 to 2024 = ((45 - 30)/30) × 100 = 50%.

Absolute revenue increase from 2021 to 2025 = 60 - 20 = 40 lakhs.

Percentage increase from 2021 to 2025 = (40/20) × 100 = 200%.

Bar graph questions often ask for comparisons, totals and ratios.

Line graph questions often ask for trends, increases, decreases and growth rates.

Important distinction: Absolute increase and percentage increase are not the same. A smaller absolute increase can represent a larger percentage increase when the starting value is smaller.

Placement tip: Check whether the vertical axis starts at zero before visually comparing bar heights or interpreting the magnitude of changes.

lessons.title: Pie Charts and Percentage Distribution
lessons.description: Calculate category values, percentage shares and angles in pie charts.
lessons.content:
A pie chart represents a whole divided into sectors. Each sector shows the proportion contributed by a category.

The complete circle represents 100% or 360 degrees.

Sector Angle = (Category Value / Total Value) × 360.

Category Value = (Category Percentage / 100) × Total Value.

Example: A company spends ₹10,00,000 annually across five categories.
Salaries = 40%
Marketing = 20%
Infrastructure = 15%
Technology = 15%
Other = 10%

Salary expenditure = 40% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹4,00,000.

Marketing expenditure = 20% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹2,00,000.

Infrastructure expenditure = ₹1,50,000.

Technology expenditure = ₹1,50,000.

Other expenditure = ₹1,00,000.

Angle representing salaries = 40/100 × 360 = 144 degrees.

Angle representing marketing = 20/100 × 360 = 72 degrees.

Ratio of salaries to marketing = 40:20 = 2:1.

Difference between salaries and infrastructure = ₹2,50,000.

If a sector's angle is 90 degrees, it represents 90/360 × 100 = 25% of the total.

Placement tip: Convert pie-chart angles into fractions or percentages before calculating actual quantities.

lessons.title: Caselet Data Interpretation and Advanced Problem Solving
lessons.description: Solve paragraph-based datasets and multi-step placement aptitude questions.
lessons.content:
Caselet Data Interpretation provides information in paragraph form instead of a ready-made table or graph. The first task is to organize the information.

Example: A placement drive includes 500 students. Of these, 40% are from Computer Science, 30% from Electronics, 20% from Mechanical and the remaining students from Civil Engineering.

Computer Science students = 40% of 500 = 200.
Electronics students = 30% of 500 = 150.
Mechanical students = 20% of 500 = 100.
Civil Engineering students = 10% of 500 = 50.

Suppose placement rates are:
Computer Science = 80%
Electronics = 60%
Mechanical = 50%
Civil Engineering = 40%.

Placed Computer Science students = 200 × 0.80 = 160.
Placed Electronics students = 150 × 0.60 = 90.
Placed Mechanical students = 100 × 0.50 = 50.
Placed Civil Engineering students = 50 × 0.40 = 20.

Total placed students = 160 + 90 + 50 + 20 = 320.

Overall placement rate = (320/500) × 100 = 64%.

Unplaced students = 500 - 320 = 180.

Advanced DI strategy:
1. Convert paragraph data into a small table.
2. Calculate missing categories using totals.
3. Separate category size from category percentage.
4. Avoid confusing percentage points with percentage change.
5. Reuse intermediate calculations across related questions.
6. Estimate first when answer options are widely separated.

Placement tip: Data Interpretation becomes easier when information is organized before solving the questions.

quizzes.question: A company has 200 employees, and 50 work in HR. What percentage work in HR?
The sales figures for four months are 20, 30, 40 and 50 units. Find the average.
Revenue increases from ₹40,000 to ₹50,000. What is the percentage increase?
In a pie chart, what percentage does a 90-degree sector represent?
Product A sells 120 units and Product B sells 80 units. What is the ratio A:B?
A company's revenue is ₹20 lakh in 2021 and ₹60 lakh in 2025. What is the percentage increase?
A pie-chart category represents 30% of a total of 600 students. How many students belong to that category?
A table shows sales of 40, 50, 60 and 70 units across four quarters. What are the total sales?
A college has 500 students. If 40% belong to Computer Science and 80% of those students are placed, how many Computer Science students are placed?
A company has 300 employees. Department A has 120 employees with 75% attendance, and Department B has 180 employees with 50% attendance. What is the overall attendance percentage?

exercises.title: Analyze Student Placement Data
exercises.description: Calculate totals, averages and percentages from placement figures.
exercises.instructions: A college records placements as follows: Computer Science = 90, Electronics = 70, Mechanical = 50 and Civil = 30. Calculate total placements, average placements per department and the percentage contribution of Computer Science.

exercises.title: Quarterly Sales Table Analysis
exercises.description: Interpret tabular sales data and calculate growth.
exercises.instructions: Quarterly sales of Product A are Q1 = 40, Q2 = 55, Q3 = 65 and Q4 = 80 units. Calculate total annual sales, average quarterly sales and the percentage increase from Q1 to Q4.

exercises.title: Bar Graph Revenue Comparison
exercises.description: Compare yearly revenue values and identify growth patterns.
exercises.instructions: A company reports revenue of ₹20 lakh, ₹30 lakh, ₹45 lakh and ₹60 lakh over four consecutive years. Calculate the total revenue, average annual revenue, largest absolute year-on-year increase and percentage growth from the first year to the fourth year.

exercises.title: Pie Chart Budget Distribution
exercises.description: Calculate actual amounts and sector angles from a budget distribution.
exercises.instructions: A company has an annual budget of ₹12,00,000. Salaries receive 40%, Marketing 25%, Technology 20% and Other Expenses 15%. Calculate the amount allocated to each category, the angle representing Technology and the difference between Salaries and Marketing.

exercises.title: Advanced Placement Data Interpretation
exercises.description: Solve a multi-stage caselet involving department sizes and placement percentages.
exercises.instructions: A college has 800 students: 35% Computer Science, 25% Electronics, 20% Mechanical and 20% Civil. Placement rates are 80%, 70%, 60% and 50% respectively. Calculate the number of students in each department, placed students in each department, total placed students, overall placement percentage and total unplaced students.
